newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury's international clout growing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury's international clout growing.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
U.S. Treasury official David Lipton was at the home of a Mexican millionaire discussing that country's future when he had an urgent phone call from Richard Holbrooke in Dayton, Ohio.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was threatening to sabotage the Yugoslav peace talks if Serbia did not get relief from Western economic sanctions, and U.S. negotiator Holbrooke asked Lipton to come to Dayton to contain the damage.

Thrust into the role of diplomat, the Treasury official succeeded in winning Milosevic's trust -- the Serbian leader wound up calling Lipton a fellow banker -- and helped bring the November 1995 talks to a successful end.

As President Bill Clinton prepares to meet this week with his fellow leaders of the industrial world at the G7 summit in Denver, Lipton and other Treasury officials are playing increasingly important roles in areas once reserved for the State Department and the Pentagon.

In early April, Robert Rubin became the first U.S. Treasury Secretary to visit Vietnam, where he signed a debt deal and also reviewed the status of Americans still missing in action in the war that ended 22 years ago. Later that month Rubin's deputy, Lawrence Summers, went before the U.S. Chamber of Commerce to tout the economic benefits of enlarging the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation military alliance.

Administration officials and private analysts ascribe the Treasury's growing influence in the international arena to a variety of factors. Some may be temporary such as the State Department's preoccupation with the Middle East in Clinton's first four-year term. Others seem more long-lasting.

"Many of the key security challenges of the post-Cold War era are economic and financial," Deputy Secretary Summers told Reuters. That is true in countries as seemingly diverse as Haiti and Russia, both struggling to build democratic societies and stabilise their economies, where the Treasury Department has played a key role in fashioning U.S. policy.

"When tax collections are a crucial element of dialogue between the United States and Russia because of the consequences of hyper-inflation in Russia or a failure to pay money due to the military, it is inevitable Treasury will be drawn in," Summers said.

Administration officials said Clinton's determination to elevate the role of economics in the foreign policy arena has also played to Treasury's advantage. So too has Treasury's role as U.S. representative at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
As Washington has cut back on bilateral foreign aid, the IMF and World Bank have become more important as financiers of developing countries and nations of the former Communist bloc.

The Treasury's growing clout has led to some grumbling at other government departments that have seen their influence wane. Summers was described by one administration official as "no shrinking violet," although he seems a much smoother operator than when Clinton first took office in 1993.

Treasury officials deny they are out to run roughshod over other government agencies and instead paint a picture of an administration where departments are less concerned with protecting turf than in working together to solve problems.

Administration officials said Treasury had benefited from weaknesses at other government agencies. The State Department under former Secretary Warren Christopher concentrated on the Middle East and gave short shrift to international economics.

After a strong start under the late Ron Brown, the Commerce Department has been preoccupied with fighting off congressional efforts first to dismantle it and then to implicate it in campaign financing scandals.

And the National Economic Council at the White House, which coordinates administration economic policy, has arguably never been as powerful since the influential Rubin left it for Treasury 2-1/2 years ago.
"Treasury is spreading its wings in a vacuum," was how one administration official put it.

Stefan-Gotz Richter, head of Transatlantic Futures, described Treasury's growing influence as "the ultimate power grab" but welcomed it nonetheless. In the post Cold War era, where U.S. involvement overseas has to be justified on economic rather than military grounds, Treasury is best placed to make the case, the economic analyst said.
"That is why on most U.S. hot spots -- Mexico, Russia and even Vietnam -- the Treasury's role before and behind the scenes just keeps on rising," Richter said.
